summary: This document specifies the Deterministic Networking (DetNet) data plane for carrying IP packets over an MPLS packet-switched network. It describes how DetNet IP flows are encapsulated so they can ride across MPLS while keeping DetNet's service properties.

plainLanguage.summary: Some messages need a reliable express delivery. This document explains how to put such delivery-promised internet messages inside another kind of network wrapper called MPLS and still keep the promise.

subtitle: How DetNet IP flows are mapped onto an MPLS network without changing the IP packets, while keeping deterministic service.

tldr.problem: DetNet offers extremely low packet loss and bounded latency to IP flows, but some of those flows have to cross an MPLS network between DetNet IP sites.
tldr.mechanism: Each DetNet IP flow is treated as an App-flow of the DetNet MPLS data plane and mapped to a single MPLS flow with an S-Label and a mandatory d-CW. Relay nodes at the edge of the MPLS domain do the mapping.
tldr.outcome: IP-encapsulated DetNet flows can ride across a DetNet MPLS network using the procedures of RFC 8964 and RFC 8939. This document adds no header information of its own.

today: RFC 9056 is a Proposed Standard (October 2021). The metadata for this site records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Deterministic Networking (DetNet) is a service a network can offer to DetNet flows. It provides delivery of data flows with extremely low packet loss rates and bounded end-to-end delivery latency. General background is in the DetNet architecture (RFC 8655).

RFC 9056 specifies use of the IP DetNet encapsulation over an MPLS network. It maps the IP data plane encapsulation described in RFC 8939 to the DetNet MPLS data plane defined in RFC 8964. Readers are assumed to know the terminology of RFC 8655 and RFC 8938.
sections.plainLanguage: Some internet messages need a promise that they arrive quickly and almost never get lost. This document shows how to carry such messages across one particular kind of road, called MPLS.

sections.title: The Overall Picture
sections.content:
End systems still originate IP-encapsulated traffic, identified as DetNet flows. An MPLS-based DetNet network sits as a sub-network between relay nodes. The relay nodes map each DetNet flow to MPLS (TE) label-switched paths (LSPs), and an IP flow is mapped to one or more pseudowires (PWs) and LSPs.

A transit node only switches on MPLS labels. It need not have any specific knowledge of the DetNet service or of the corresponding DetNet flow identification.

The RFC describes two scenarios. In the first, relay nodes sit at the edge of the MPLS domain and so act like Terminating Provider Edges (T-PEs). In the second, relay nodes provide service protection over the MPLS domain: R1 and R3 are similar to T-PEs and R2, in the middle, is similar to a Switching Provider Edge (S-PE). If the end systems are not DetNet aware, the edge nodes act as DetNet service proxies, initiating and terminating DetNet service for the application's IP flows. Data plane processing is essentially the same for relays and edges, though control plane operation is likely to differ.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages travel from a sender, through an edge helper who loads them into the special truck, along the road, and out through another helper. The road workers in the middle only read the truck's label, not what is inside.

sections.title: The Encapsulation
sections.content:
The basic approach is to treat a DetNet IP flow as an App-flow from the DetNet MPLS point of view. The IP packet, with the next-protocol fields described in RFC 8939, becomes the payload. A DetNet Control Word (d-CW) and the MPLS labels go on top, and then whatever link or sub-network encapsulation is used, such as L2, TSN or UDP over IP.

The DetNet MPLS data plane uses a single S-Label to support a single App-flow, and RFC 8939 identifies a single DetNet flow from IP and next-level protocol header information. RFC 8939 also defines flow aggregation through prefixes, wildcards, lists and port ranges. Together these give fairly straightforward procedures. Mapping is similar for DetNet IP flows and plain IP flows: the six-tuple of IP is mapped to the S-Label in both cases, and fields may be mapped or ignored when going from IP to MPLS.

Compared with plain MPLS there are three main differences: flow identification is mandatory for the forwarding decision (it is not based on a FEC), the d-CW is mandatory, and DetNet-specific treatment is needed while forwarding over the DetNet MPLS network.
sections.plainLanguage: The original message goes in a box with a special tag, and then the box gets the truck's address labels. The tag and the labels are always required, so the truck always knows which promise to keep.

sections.title: Flow Identification and Traffic Treatment
sections.content:
At the ingress, a relay node (ingress T-PE) MUST map a DetNet IP flow, as identified in RFC 8939, into a single MPLS DetNet flow and process it following RFC 8964. Packet Replication Function (PRF) MAY be supported at the MPLS level, and aggregation MAY be supported as RFC 8964 defines. The mapping of IP flows to MPLS flows MUST be provisionable via configuration, for example from the Controller Plane.

At the egress, a relay node (egress T-PE) MAY be provisioned to treat packets from the DetNet MPLS data plane as DetNet IP flows. A single incoming MPLS flow MAY be treated as a single DetNet IP flow without examining IP headers, or the packets MAY follow the normal DetNet IP flow identification procedures of RFC 8939. An implementation MUST support configuring this handling. Layer 4 transport use, for example for multipath, is out of scope.

Traffic treatment for a flow is provisioned by configuration or the Controller Plane. When sending over DetNet MPLS, a relay node MUST ensure the provisioned treatment is provided at the forwarding sub-layer as RFC 8964 describes. Treatment for IP flows received over MPLS MUST follow RFC 8939.
sections.plainLanguage: The first helper must put each promised message into exactly one truck lane. The last helper can either take the message out as an ordinary one or keep treating it as a truck package, depending on how they were told to behave.

sections.title: Management and Control Information
sections.content:
At the MPLS ingress node, two pieces of information are needed. First, how each MPLS App-flow is selected from incoming IP traffic, using the identification information of RFC 8939, including wildcards, port ranges and the ability to ignore specific IP fields. Second, which DetNet MPLS service should carry the matching traffic, as described in RFC 8964, including service and traffic delivery information.

At the MPLS egress node, the node needs the S-Label value that identifies the encapsulated App-flow, and for each S-Label how received traffic is handled: as other DetNet IP traffic, or directly as an MPLS App-flow for further processing under RFC 8964.

The DetNet Controller Plane is responsible for provisioning both the flow identification information and the flow-specific resources needed for the traffic treatment, for aggregated and individual flows alike.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone in charge has to tell the helpers which messages go in which truck lane and what to do with them at the other end.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
General DetNet security considerations are in RFC 9055, and DetNet MPLS and DetNet IP considerations (RFC 8964, RFC 8939) apply equally. From a data plane perspective, this document does not add or modify any header information.

The main data plane concerns are keeping data integrity and delivering the DetNet service. Application flows can be protected by the underlying technology, for example IPsec for IP flows or MACsec for IP-over-Ethernet flows.

At the management and control level, DetNet flows are identified per flow, which may give Controller Plane attackers more information about data flows. The RFC calls this inherent to DetNet. To keep the service available, provisions can be made against DoS and delay attacks, such as policing and shaping at the input of a DetNet domain, and authentication and authorization of devices to mitigate man-in-the-middle attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: This document does not change any labels, so it adds no new risks of its own. The usual safeguards still apply, like locks on the truck and checking who is allowed in the delivery network.
